entities.name: Adeodatus II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pope Adeodatus II (reigned 672–676) led the Roman Church at a moment of relative institutional stabilisation after the turbulent mid-seventh century controversies over Monothelitism — the doctrinal dispute about whether Christ had one or two wills, which had divided the Eastern and Western Churches and generated fierce political and theological conflict. His pontificate came in the aftermath of the Lateran Council of 649 (which had condemned Monothelitism) and before the decisive resolution at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).

Adeodatus II's four-year pontificate is notable primarily for the administrative measures he took to regularise Church life in Rome and for his concern for the poor and pilgrim communities in the city. His charity toward pilgrims — Rome was a major pilgrimage destination — reflected the pastoral priorities of a pope who oversaw the city's religious infrastructure. His pontificate was conducted in close relationship with the Byzantine imperial court, which still formally recognised the emperor's role in confirming papal elections.

His reign represented the papacy's gradual accumulation of independence and institutional strength in the period between the Gregorian papacy and the more assertive pontificates of the eighth and ninth centuries. The popes of this transitional period, including Adeodatus II, built the administrative and pastoral foundations on which the medieval papacy's greater authority would rest.
